sweep_summary: Four target items, none openly available: Kamprath 1987 (UT Austin diss.) exists only on ProQuest (8717451; record saved, no abstract) - priority high; Roca 1999 (De Gruyter, doi 10.1515/9783110197082.2.659, JS-walled) - medium; Anderson 2011 and Maiden 2011 (OUP Morphological Autonomy, pp. 12-35 and 36-50, an automated-access block-walled, Semantic Scholar CLOSED) - their 2008 OxMorph1 workshop abstracts were recovered from arquivo.pt and. Anderson's abstract presupposes the deciding source's stress-keyed stem alternation, Maiden's is a morphomic (non-phonological) argument silent on stress placement. Bonus first-hand find, downloaded and read: Kamprath 1986 LSA paper (ERIC ED287300, archive.org scan) on Berguen Romansh, which refines the catalog (unstressed vowels reduce exceptionlessly to [i]/[u]/[ə]; at most two stresses per word, one per lexical level) but gives no placement rule, so Anderson 2008 stays the deciding source (catalog's classification 'weight' stands). Web.archive.org, cowgill.ling.yale.edu, OpenAlex, Google Books and web search were all unavailable by automated download; everything downloaded is under with and a addendum.

new_statements.quote: In Bergüner-Romansh, stress can fall on more than one syllable within a word, an indication that the stress application rule applies more than once. [...] It is evident that the first syllable is stressed because the vowel there is not reduced: it has not undergone the exceptionless rule by which vowels in unstressed syllables are reduced to either [i], [u], or [ə] (Figure 2). [p. 9:] These data, like the nominal data, support our claim that stress applies a maximum of twice in a word, but not with every affixation. That is, it applies not cyclically but once per lexical level.

It supports the catalog's full-vs-reduced-vowel weight class and shows that the second stress in Berguen words is a morphological (lexical-level) stress, refining the catalog's note that contrasts Anderson's initial-syllable secondary with StressTyp2's Kamprath-based 'all heavy syllables + alternating'. new_statements.quote: An extensive system of stress-conditioned vowel alternations has developed in the history of this form of Rumantsch from purely phonological status to that of phonologically conditioned allomorphy. [...] Synchronically, Surmiran stems must in general have two listed forms, one used when primary stress falls on the last vowel of the stem and the other when this vowel will not bear primary stress. This pattern is most thoroughly exemplified in the verbal system, but in this talk I will discuss its effects elsewhere in the morphology, responding in part to comments by Maiden on earlier presentations of the system.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Romansh has an empty rule; the existing Kamprath 1986 statement (Berguen) gives the full-vs-reduced-vowel diagnostic of stress and says stress can apply twice. Anderson's abstract is compatible: it confirms for Surmiran that primary stress is not fixed at one syllable but moves between the stem-final vowel and the ending across a paradigm, with the stem vowel reduced/alternated when unstressed (the same full-vs-reduced-vowel correlate). It agrees with WALS's coding of Romansch (Surmeiran) as 'No fixed stress'. Nothing contradicts the catalog. Describes Surmiran, not Berguen.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated. The abstract says that in Surmiran a single primary stress falls on the last vowel of the stem in some inflectional forms and off the stem (on the ending) in others, i.e. primary stress is mobile within the paradigm and its position is decided by the morphological form, not by a fixed syllable count; the stem vowel is full when stressed and reduced/alternated when unstressed. Which forms are stem-stressed vs ending-stressed is not said in the abstract (the full chapter presumably gives it).
new_statements.exceptions: 'words whose base contains only a single stem form' (non-alternating stems, mostly loans, e.g. from German) are flagged as of particular interest but not described
new_statements.identity_note: Anderson 2011 and Maiden 2011 describe Surmiran (Rumantsch Surmiran, Oberhalbstein/Surses), and WALS's 'Romansch (Surmeiran)' datapoints coded from Roca 1999 and Kamprath 1987 are the same variety (Kamprath's field dialect is Berguen, a Surmiran-adjacent dialect of the Albula valley). The existing catalog statements (Kamprath 1986, Lutta 1923) are about Berguen. Nothing opened covers Sursilvan, Sutsilvan, Puter, Vallader or Rumantsch Grischun.

new_statements.quote: With the exception of some synchronically foreign words, main stress falls on the penult if the rhyme of the final syllable consists of [@], possibly followed by [r], [l] [n] or [s]. If the final rhyme contains a full (non-@) vowel, or [@] followed by some other consonant, the main stress falls on this syllable instead. Assuming that syllables whose rhyme is of the first sort (nucleus [@] with coda limited to [r,l,n,s]) are prosodically weak, and others strong, we can describe this simply by the rule in (). () Main Stress Rule: Build a quantity-sensitive trochee at the right edge of the word.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (weight; Anderson 2008 section 2.2 rule: penult if final rhyme is schwa (+r/l/n/s), else final): this is the same author's restatement, adding the explicit foot-based formulation ('quantity-sensitive trochee at the right edge'), the Rightmost tie-break and the initial-syllable secondary stress. Consistent with the Kamprath 1986 statement held by the project (full vs reduced vowels diagnose stress; compound members stressed separately) and with WALS 15A right-edge ultimate/penultimate. Describes Surmiran.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Surmiran main stress: a quantity-sensitive trochee at the right word edge. Final syllables whose rhyme is schwa alone or schwa + r/l/n/s are weak, so stress goes to the penult; any other final syllable (full vowel, or schwa + another consonant) is strong and takes the stress. Where both footings are possible a Rightmost preference gives final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 8: 'Secondary stress falls on initial syllables (usually) separated by at least one syllable from the main stress; parts of compounds are stressed separately with main stress on the stress center of the final element. Other secondary stresses appear to be the result of cyclic word formation'; the author does not formulate a full secondary-stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: 'some synchronically foreign words' (loans, especially German) have exceptional stress; unstressed [E, O] 'not rare' in unstressed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Anderson 2011 = Surmiran (Savognin area, central Grisons); Maiden 2011 = Romansh varieties generally (abstract names Romansh only); Roca 1999 = 'Rhaeto-Romance (Romanish)', per WALS the Surmeiran data after Kamprath 1987 (Berguen/Bravuogn); the survey ch. 7 spells it 'Romanish'/'Romanisch'.

readall_conflicts: Anderson (abstract) says Surmiran primary stress alternates between the stem-final vowel and the ending across paradigms; Maiden (abstract) disputes only whether the resulting vowel alternations are synchronically stress-conditioned or morphomic, not the stress positions themselves. WALS (from Kamprath 1987 and Roca 1999) codes Surmiran as no fixed stress, right-edge ultimate/penultimate, combined weight factors, which fits the already-recorded Berguen statements (Lutta 1923 p. 38: word accent always on the last vowel of the word that can bear it; Kamprath 1986: unstressed vowels reduce exceptionlessly). The only open issue is the one already noted in the catalog: how many stresses a word carries (Kamprath's second, lexical-level stress in Berguen vs a single primary stress in Anderson's Surmiran description), which is a variety difference and a level-of-description difference, not a contradiction about primary-stress placement.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage and rule (7) are verbatim at the stated place in the held Anderson 2008 ms (section 2.2, ms p. 7), and the supporting Haiman & Beninca 1992 pp. 56-58 passage is verbatim in the OAPEN PDF text we hold. Deciding source: a 2008 peer-reviewed article by the leading specialist on Surmiran with an explicit synchronic stress rule (quantity-sensitive trochee at the right edge; final schwa(+r/l/n/s) light), backed by a 1992 reference survey; independent lines agree: StressTyp2/Kamprath 1987 via Hayes 1995 ('final if heavy, else penult'), Lutta 1923 (downloaded now: word accent on the last vowel able to bear it, reduced vowels never stressed), and Maurer-Cecchini 2021's Sursilvan spelling rules (consonant-final other than -n/-s = final stress; vowel/-n/-s-final = penult). Nothing found suggests the 'weight, right edge, full-vs-reduced-vowel' coding is wrong. Residual gaps are (a) Kamprath 198

tone.quote: again, we are dealing with a kind of alternation which is nearly universal in the synchronic phonology of stress languages (see Haiman 1972), but which has become conventionalized in a number of Romance languages, among them—although in varying degrees—the Rhaeto-Romance dialects. For example, when Huonder (1901:518) or Kamprath (1985) reports that in Surselvan or Surmeiran, the seven-vowel system of stressed syllables reduces to /i, ə, u/ in unstressed syllables in general, it is clear we are dealing with a productive set of alternations which we could expect to find in almost any stress language, and which are of typological rather than historical interest.

sources.quote: Some recent studies (e.g., by Burzio on palatal-velar alternation in Italian verbs, and a forthcoming paper by S. Anderson, on apparent stress conditioning of allomorphy in Romansh) propose that what I believe to be morphomic patterns in the Romance verb are phonologically conditioned. My paper will be a discussion of the boundary between the morphomic and the phonologically conditioned. Through close analysis of data drawn in particular from Romansh, I shall show that the view that they are phonologically conditioned is often misleading, and the product of an overly phonologizing perspective on morphology.
